caseName: San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments v. Sahagun
citation: Los Angeles County Superior Court, Case No. 19STCV22715
court: Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles
keyFacts: SGVCOG took a commercial property in Montebello in fee for a Union Pacific Railroad grade-separation/safety project. The owner claimed roughly $3.5 million in lost business goodwill in addition to the land value; the agency's final pre-trial settlement offer and expert valuation were both close to the eventual verdict.
outcome: Jury awarded just compensation reported at approximately $1,372,000 for the fee taking, coming in under 6% above the agency's own expert valuation and below the agency's final pre-trial offer; the jury rejected the owner's ~$3.5M lost-goodwill claim, reportedly on failure-to-mitigate grounds.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for fee-simple taking of commercial property, exclusive of the separately-claimed and ultimately rejected business-goodwill damages
notes: The $1,372,000 figure appears consistently in secondary AI-search synthesis of the law firm's (Burke, Williams & Sorensen) press release, but the primary release could not be directly fetched (blocked/timed out) to verify the exact figure firsthand. Useful example of a goodwill claim being defeated entirely on mitigation grounds rather than reduced.

caseName: North Carolina Department of Transportation v. AJA Investments
citation: Moore County Superior Court, Case No. 23 CVS 1525
court: Superior Court of Moore County, North Carolina
keyFacts: NCDOT condemned a 2.18-acre commercial parcel improved with two income-producing industrial buildings (~10,261 sq ft total) for a highway-widening project, taking 0.667 acres in fee plus permanent and temporary easements and requiring demolition of both structures, leaving a remnant parcel with severely limited development potential.
outcome: Settled for $1,150,000, exceeding NCDOT's highest initial offer of $693,800 by $456,200.
dollarAmountBasis: Negotiated settlement of just compensation for fee-simple right-of-way taking plus permanent utility easement and temporary construction easement, including loss of two demolished industrial buildings
notes: Clean, well-documented example of the gap between a DOT's initial statutory deposit offer and negotiated final compensation (66% increase) for a small industrial/commercial property.

caseName: Colorado Department of Transportation v. Mickels
citation: Jefferson County District Court (exact case number not disclosed in press coverage)
court: District Court, Jefferson County, Colorado
keyFacts: CDOT sought to acquire 17 acres adjoining an I-70 wildlife underpass project near Genesee, CO, to prevent development of the land. The 81-year-old owner, Jeri Mickels, rejected CDOT's initial offer as inadequate; CDOT pursued a condemnation action and the case went to a jury valuation trial, with the owner's realtor providing comparable-sales evidence.
outcome: Jury sided with the property owner's valuation; CDOT ordered to pay roughly $3 million total, of which approximately $2.3 million went to the owner and the remainder covered attorney fees and court costs under Colorado's fee-shifting eminent domain rules.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury-determined just compensation paid directly to the property owner for the 17-acre taking (excludes the separate attorney-fee/cost award that brought CDOT's total outlay to ~$3 million)
notes: Local news coverage did not include CDOT's original offer amount or a formal case caption/number, so this could not be independently cross-checked against a court record.

caseName: Virginia Department of Transportation v. [national retailer, name not disclosed] (Fairfax County highway-entrance closure)
citation: Circuit Court, Fairfax County, Virginia (case caption/number not disclosed by reporting firm)
court: Circuit Court of Fairfax County, Virginia
keyFacts: VDOT closed a national retail chain's highway entrance/access point in Fairfax County to build a highway overpass, impairing the store's customer access. VDOT's compensation offer for the access impairment was $115,000.
outcome: Jury awarded the retailer $5.6 million in just compensation for the loss of access — nearly 50 times VDOT's offer.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for loss of highway access/frontage value to a retail commercial property (access/severance damages, not a land taking)
notes: Sourced from the representing law firm's own case-results page, which does not disclose the formal case name, docket number, or exact trial date; the year is an estimate. Included because the dollar spread (offer vs. verdict) is a striking, real, and frequently-cited data point for access/severance-damage disputes, one of the least appellate-documented sub-categories of eminent domain.

caseName: State v. Gleannloch Commercial Development, LP
citation: 585 S.W.3d 509 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2019)
court: Court of Appeals of Texas, First District, Houston
keyFacts: TxDOT condemned portions of two commercial reserve parcels fronting a master-planned residential development for construction of the Grand Parkway (SH 99) in Harris County. The parcels were held for commercial/retail development.
outcome: Jury awarded $19.4 million in combined just compensation for the two parcels — 292% above the State's combined initial offer, representing 100% of the compensation the landowner sought at trial. Judgment affirmed on appeal.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined jury verdict for two consolidated commercial-reserve parcel takings, affirmed on appeal
notes: Published appellate opinion with a full, independently verifiable citation — one of the stronger data points in this set, and useful for showing how large the gap between a DOT's statutory offer and a full jury verdict can run for development-ready commercial land along a major highway project.

caseName: Williamson County, Texas v. J.A. Davidson Holdings, L.P.
citation: Williamson County District Court (exact case number not confirmed)
court: District Court, Williamson County, Texas
keyFacts: Williamson County condemned land from J.A. Davidson Holdings for a county roadway project in a fast-growing part of the Austin metro area. One portion of the property went to a jury trial; a second, related portion was resolved by negotiated settlement after the verdict.
outcome: Jury awarded $4,437,000 for the tried portion (exceeding the county's presented valuation); the parties then resolved the remaining property dispute via a Rule 11 settlement agreement for an additional $2,913,000, bringing the combined recovery to approximately $7.35 million.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined total of jury verdict ($4,437,000) plus negotiated Rule 11 settlement ($2,913,000) covering two related takings from the same roadway project
notes: Local news source; a full case number/citation was not located to cross-check against the Williamson County docket.

caseName: State v. Moore Outdoor Properties, LP / Arrington Outdoor of Fort Worth, L.P.
citation: No. 08-12-00034-CV (Tex. App.—El Paso, Nov. 13, 2013) (transferred from Fort Worth)
court: Court of Appeals of Texas, El Paso (sitting for the Second District, Fort Worth)
keyFacts: TxDOT condemned land along I-30 in Fort Worth for a highway project, taking a commercial billboard structure (two 15'x60' faces) along with the underlying leasehold/permit rights that Arrington had purchased for $1,268,454 in 2006. The Special Commissioners' initial joint award to the two claimants was only $334,194.
outcome: After a jury trial, Arrington was awarded $969,243 for its leasehold and billboard-structure interest (affirmed on appeal); Moore Outdoor Properties separately settled for $480,000.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for the value of a commercial billboard leasehold/structure taken for a highway project, affirmed on appeal
notes: A useful, less-common commercial-property-type data point (outdoor advertising/signage leasehold rather than land or a building) with a full published citation and multiple cross-checkable dollar figures (purchase price, initial commissioners' award, settlement, and jury verdict).

caseName: Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Inglewood Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 2122
citation: Los Angeles County Superior Court (exact case number not confirmed)
court: Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles
keyFacts: LA Metro condemned the Florence Avenue building housing Inglewood VFW Post 2122 (in the post's home for more than 80 years) to clear the path for the Crenshaw/LAX light-rail extension into the South Bay. Metro's initial offer of $650,000 was, per the post's counsel, insufficient to purchase a replacement building in the community for its roughly 320 members.
outcome: Jury awarded the veterans post $3,357,323 in just compensation, more than $2.7 million above Metro's initial offer.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for just compensation for a fee-simple taking of a nonprofit-owned commercial/institutional building
notes: Sourced from the representing firm's case-results page rather than a court record; exact trial date and docket number not independently confirmed. Included as a real example of a public-benefit/institutional commercial building taking with a large offer-to-verdict spread.

caseName: City of North Canton v. Julius Brown, LLC
citation: Case No. 2024CA00030 (Ohio Ct. App., 5th Dist., Jan. 6, 2025)
court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Fifth Appellate District
keyFacts: The City of North Canton condemned commercial buildings for a road-widening project and valued the buildings at $0 in its case; the trial court excluded the owner's county-auditor tax-valuation evidence (which showed a value difference of over $300,000 with vs. without the buildings) and the owner's appraiser opinion ($45/sq ft), and the jury returned a $0 verdict for the buildings at the first trial.
outcome: The Fifth District reversed, holding that county-auditor property-tax valuations are admissible evidence in an eminent-domain trial to help the jury determine fair compensation, and remanded for a new compensation trial.
dollarAmountBasis: No final dollar figure yet — first trial produced a $0 jury verdict for the condemned buildings, which the appellate court vacated/remanded because favorable tax-valuation evidence had been wrongly excluded
notes: Rare disclosed example of a condemning authority's own valuation position being $0 for standing commercial improvements, and of a jury actually returning a $0 verdict before being overturned on evidentiary grounds. Illustrates how big an evidentiary ruling (admissibility of tax-assessment evidence) can swing a compensation outcome; final retrial figure not yet available.

caseName: Medical Acquisition Company, Inc. v. Superior Court (Tri-City Healthcare District)
citation: 20 Cal. App. 5th 34, D072509 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, Jan. 11, 2018)
court: California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division One
keyFacts: Tri-City Healthcare District used California's constitutional 'quick-take' procedure to take immediate possession of a partially completed medical office building, making a pretrial possession deposit of $4.7 million, which the owner (MAC) withdrew. The case then proceeded to a compensation trial roughly three years later.
outcome: The jury found the property's fair market value to be $16.83 million — nearly 3.6x the quick-take deposit — and separately awarded MAC $2,933,700 for the district's breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. The court ordered the district to increase its deposit by about $12.2 million to match the verdict, and the Court of Appeal addressed the novel procedural question of what security/bonding the owner could be required to post to withdraw the increased post-judgment deposit.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury-determined fair market value of the condemned medical office building, compared against the condemning agency's $4.7 million quick-take possession deposit
notes: Strong, fully-citable example of the core risk in quick-take procedures for commercial property: an agency can take immediate possession on a fraction of what a jury later determines is owed, and the owner then has to litigate over withdrawal/bonding conditions on the gap.

caseName: Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Alameda Produce Market, LLC
court: Supreme Court of California
keyFacts: LA Metro used the quick-take procedure in 2004 to acquire a downtown Los Angeles commercial property (produce market) later developed into a bus depot facility, over the owner's objection to the validity of Metro's resolution of necessity. The owner (and later its lender) withdrew the quick-take deposit while continuing to litigate the right-to-take challenge; the case reached the California Supreme Court on whether withdrawing the deposit waived that challenge.
outcome: The California Supreme Court held that a party's withdrawal of a quick-take deposit does not, by itself, waive the right to continue challenging the condemnor's right to take. The underlying valuation dispute was ultimately resolved through a confidential settlement in 2011 after the property owner's parent entity went through bankruptcy, ending seven years of litigation.
dollarAmountBasis: No public dollar figure disclosed — final resolution was a confidential settlement paying the appraised value of the property less the already-withdrawn deposit, per court filings, but the specific number was not made public
notes: Leading California quick-take doctrine case (deposit withdrawal does not waive a right-to-take challenge); included despite the lack of a disclosed settlement figure because it is one of the most-cited quick-take procedural precedents and shows how a right-to-take fight can drag a compensation dispute out for years (here, seven) with the property already in agency hands the whole time.

caseName: PKO Ventures, LLC v. Norfolk Redevelopment & Housing Authority (Norva Properties)
court: Supreme Court of Virginia
keyFacts: Norfolk Redevelopment and Housing Authority sought to condemn the headquarters site of Norva Plastics (owned by Howard Everton, through PKO Ventures/Norva Properties) as part of a redevelopment project near Old Dominion University, relying on a blight-based redevelopment designation. At the trial-court compensation phase, a jury had awarded the owner approximately $3.4-3.75 million, but the owner separately challenged whether NRHA had the legal authority to take the property at all.
outcome: The Virginia Supreme Court unanimously held NRHA had no right to take the property because it was not validly part of a blighted redevelopment area, voiding the condemnation and ordering the property returned to the owner — mooting the earlier jury compensation verdict since no taking occurred.
dollarAmountBasis: Not applicable — the condemnation itself was voided on appeal, so no compensation was ultimately owed despite an earlier jury having valued the taking at roughly $3.4-3.75 million
notes: Closest fit among the four required claim-type buckets is 'quick_take_challenge,' though this is more precisely a right-to-take / blight-designation validity challenge (explicitly in the requested scope) rather than a quick-take deposit/possession dispute. Included because it is a rare example of a successful blight-designation challenge that completely zeroed out an already-adjudicated compensation award — a materially different outcome pattern than a valuation dispute, and important for the valuation tool to flag as a possible full-defense outcome. The $3.4M vs. $3.75M discrepancy in secondary sources for the earlier, later-voided jury verdict could not be resolved from available reporting.

caseName: Summit Carbon Solutions, LLC v. Malloy
citation: North Dakota Supreme Court (decided January 2025)
court: Supreme Court of North Dakota
keyFacts: Summit Carbon Solutions sought pre-condemnation survey access to a landowner's property under North Dakota's survey-access statute to plan a CO2 pipeline route, ahead of any actual condemnation filing. The landowner denied permission and challenged the company's statutory survey-access authority.
outcome: The North Dakota Supreme Court upheld Summit Carbon Solutions' right to conduct pre-condemnation surveys over the landowner's objection.
dollarAmountBasis: No compensation at issue — dispute was limited to survey-access authority, not valuation
notes: No dollar figure exists for this claim type by design — pre-condemnation survey-access disputes are fought over statutory/constitutional authority to enter land, not over compensation amounts (compensation for any survey-caused damage is typically a separate, later claim). Included for jurisdictional diversity and because it mirrors the fact pattern of the site's already-tracked PSEG Renewable Transmission case.

caseName: Texas Rice Land Partners, Ltd. v. Denbury Green Pipeline-Texas, LLC
court: Supreme Court of Texas
keyFacts: Denbury Green Pipeline, a CO2 pipeline operator, checked a box on a state form to self-designate as a 'common carrier' with eminent domain power, then attempted to survey and later condemn an easement across Texas Rice Land Partners' land without the landowner's consent. The landowner challenged whether Denbury genuinely qualified as a common carrier entitled to eminent-domain/survey authority in the first place.
outcome: The Texas Supreme Court held that simply checking a box on a state regulatory form does not conclusively establish common-carrier (and thus eminent domain) status; a landowner may challenge that status in court, and the entity bears the burden of proving a reasonable probability that the pipeline will serve the public rather than solely the owner's own affiliated interests. Remanded for further proceedings on Denbury's actual common-carrier status.
dollarAmountBasis: No compensation at issue in this appeal — dispute was over the threshold question of eminent-domain/common-carrier authority
notes: Foundational, widely-cited Texas precedent establishing that a company's self-declared 'common carrier' status is not conclusive and can be challenged before it may exercise survey/condemnation authority over commercial or agricultural land — directly on point for the pre-condemnation-access-dispute claim type even though it does not carry a dollar figure.

caseName: In re Elba Express Co., LLC Petitions for Ex Parte Survey Entry
citation: Court of Common Pleas, Hampton and Colleton Counties, South Carolina (approx. 88+ separate petitions, 2026, ongoing)
court: Courts of Common Pleas, Hampton County and Colleton County, South Carolina
keyFacts: Elba Express, planning a 71-mile interstate gas pipeline from Screven County, Georgia to Canadys, South Carolina (to feed a proposed 2,200-megawatt Dominion Energy/Santee Cooper power plant on a former coal-plant site), sent repeated written notices (Sept. 2025, Dec. 2025, and April 2026) to landowners along the route seeking survey access and, when refused, filed roughly 88 separate 'Petition for Ex Parte Order to Enter Onto Real Property' actions against individual landowners across Hampton and Colleton Counties (with about 100 total filings including Georgia). A landowner with three parcels on the route responded by filing a proposed class action against Elba Express seeking to represent up to 94 similarly-situated owners.
outcome: Ongoing as of mid-2026; no rulings on the merits reported yet.
dollarAmountBasis: No compensation at issue yet — matter is at the pre-survey access stage, well before any condemnation valuation proceeding
notes: Current, real, and unusually well-documented example of mass pre-condemnation survey-access litigation at scale (dozens of individual ex parte petitions plus a proposed landowner class action) tied to a commercial energy-infrastructure project; included for both currency and volume even though no dollar outcome exists yet.

caseName: PSEG Renewable Transmission LLC v. Arentz Family, LP
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
keyFacts: PSEG Renewable Transmission sought pre-certification survey access to 117 landowners' properties along the proposed 67-mile, 500kV Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project transmission line, relying on Md. Code Ann., Real Property Section 12-111, before the Maryland Public Service Commission had issued the certificate of public convenience and necessity the project ultimately needs.
outcome: The Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction letting PSEG enter the properties to survey, holding PSEG qualified as an entity with eminent domain power under the statute even without a completed certification, and holding a temporary survey entry is not itself a compensable physical taking.
dollarAmountBasis: No compensation at issue — dispute was over survey-access authority prior to any condemnation filing
notes: Already tracked on the CREdocket site (case id live-028) as of this research; included here for completeness of the eminent-domain research set since it is directly on point for the pre_condemnation_access_dispute claim type and involves commercial/agricultural landowners along a utility corridor.

caseName: Lost Tree Village Corp. v. United States
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
keyFacts: Lost Tree Village Corporation, a real estate development company, owned a roughly 4.99-acre upland parcel (Plat 57) in Florida intended for a single high-end residential/commercial development lot. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers denied the Clean Water Act Section 404 permit needed to fill wetlands for access, citing environmental concerns, which the company alleged destroyed the parcel's economic value (from an estimated $4.2 million to about $27,500 — a 99.4% diminution).
outcome: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' finding that the permit denial was a categorical (Lucas-type) regulatory taking of the parcel, entitling the owner to compensation for the full pre-denial value.
dollarAmountBasis: Compensation ordered equal to the parcel's appraised value immediately before the permit denial that the courts found effected a total regulatory taking
notes: One of the strongest disclosed-dollar regulatory-takings precedents available; the property was held by a commercial real estate development company as part of a larger development project (not a personal residence), making it a good fit for the tool's commercial-property scope even though it was zoned for eventual residential use.

caseName: DeVillier v. Texas
court: Supreme Court of the United States
keyFacts: TxDOT raised a concrete median barrier on Interstate 10 near Houston to use the highway as a flood-evacuation route, which functioned as a dam and repeatedly flooded farms, ranches, and other land (including working agricultural/commercial operations) to the north during Hurricane Harvey and Tropical Storm Imelda. Landowners sued Texas directly under the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause; Texas argued there was no direct federal cause of action against a state for a taking absent an enabling state-law vehicle.
outcome: The Supreme Court unanimously held the case should proceed under the cause of action available under Texas law rather than a freestanding federal one, vacating and remanding for the claims to continue in the lower courts; the case did not resolve or disclose any compensation figure.
dollarAmountBasis: No compensation figure — decision addressed only the procedural cause-of-action question and remanded for further proceedings
notes: Included as a landmark, currently-unresolved regulatory/inverse-condemnation-by-flooding case directly relevant to infrastructure-driven takings claims against commercial and agricultural land; no dollar amount exists yet because the merits compensation question was remanded rather than decided.

caseName: Sheetz v. County of El Dorado, California
court: Supreme Court of the United States
keyFacts: El Dorado County conditioned a building permit on payment of a $23,420 legislatively-set traffic-impact mitigation fee. The applicant argued the fee was an unconstitutional exaction under Nollan/Dolan because the county never made an individualized determination that his specific project caused $23,420 in traffic impact.
outcome: The Supreme Court unanimously held that the Nollan/Dolan 'unconstitutional conditions' framework applies to permit conditions imposed by legislation, not just individualized administrative conditions, rejecting the county's argument that legislatively-set fees are categorically exempt from heightened takings scrutiny. Remanded for further proceedings on whether this specific fee satisfies Nollan/Dolan.
dollarAmountBasis: The disputed traffic-impact mitigation fee itself, which is the amount at stake pending the remand determination of whether it is a valid exaction
notes: The underlying permit was for a single-family residence rather than a commercial project, so this is included primarily for its direct and immediate relevance to commercial development impact/exaction fees generally (the same legislatively-set-fee exaction framework applies to commercial permits in the same counties), not as a commercial-property fact pattern itself. The $23,420 figure is the disputed fee amount, not a final compensation award — the case was remanded.

caseName: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission v. United States
court: Supreme Court of the United States; on remand, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
keyFacts: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' deviations from an approved water-release plan at a dam caused repeated, government-induced flooding of the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission's Dave Donaldson Black River Wildlife Management Area over a six-year period, killing timber and altering the land's usable character. The Court of Federal Claims initially awarded $5.7 million for lost timber and reforestation costs; the Federal Circuit reversed, holding temporary flooding could never be a taking; the Supreme Court reversed that categorical rule.
outcome: The Supreme Court held 8-0 that temporary, government-induced flooding is not automatically exempt from Takings Clause liability and remanded for a multi-factor analysis; on remand, the Federal Circuit affirmed that a compensable taking had occurred and upheld the original damages calculation.
dollarAmountBasis: Court of Federal Claims' original damages award (lost timber value plus reforestation costs) for recurring temporary flooding, ultimately upheld after the Supreme Court remand
notes: The condemned/damaged land here is a state-owned wildlife management area rather than privately-held commercial real estate, so its fit with the tool's 'commercial property' scope is imperfect. Included anyway because it is the landmark methodology precedent for temporary/recurring regulatory-flooding takings damages (the same framework courts apply to flooding claims against commercial and industrial land, as in the pending DeVillier line of cases), and because it is one of the few regulatory-takings cases in this set with a disclosed, court-tested dollar figure.
